To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the exposure of isolated osteclasts to elevated ambient calcium concentrations ([Ca2+]a) inhibits bone resorption and acid phosphatase release.
divalent cations mimic the effect of extracellular calcium in inhibiting bone resorption.

the exposure of isolated osteoblasts to elevated extracellular ionised levels of calcium ([Ca2+])e) inhibited bone formation and alkaline phosphatase release, and that these effects were mimicked by the divalent cation, magnesium.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of calcium in bone resorption and the mechanism by which it exerts its influence on osteoclasts.
a better understanding of the mechanisms involved in osteoclastic bone resorption, with the aim of developing novel therapeutic agents for the treatment of bone disease.
the mechanisms by which osteoclasts regulate their activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of [Ca2]e on bone resorbing osteclast is mediated by a “calcium sensor” which is located at the cell membrane, and which can also be activated by other divalent cationic compounds.
the effects of [Ca2+], Mg2+ or Ba2+ on the osteoclasts are due to a direct action on the cell membrane and not to a passive change in intracellular calcium concentration.
the effect of [Ca2]e on osteoclastic bone resorption is mediated by a surface membrane “receptor” that can be activated by divalent cations other than calcium.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
extracellular Ca2+ and other divalent cation ions can mimic the effect of ionomycin, suggesting a “calcium‐receptor‐like” mechanism of action.
extracellular calcium ions (or other divalent cation ions) can influence osteoclast activity by a direct action on the osteoclast membrane.

the effects of extracellular Ca2+ on osteoclasts are mimicked by Mg2+ and Ba2+ but not by Sr2+, Mn2+ or Cd2+, and that the effects of Ca2+, Mg2+, and Ba2+ on osteoblasts are mimiced by Sr2+ and Mn2+ but not Ca2+, Mg 2+, or Ba2+.
The main takeaway from our work is that
osteoclasts are responsive to divalent cation levels and that the effect of extracellular calcium on osteoclasts can be mimicked by other cations.
the effects of [Ca2]e on osteoclastic bone resorption are mediated by a surface receptor that binds Ca2+ and other divalent cation species.
divalent cations can mimic the inhibitory effects of elevated extracellular calcium on bone resorbing activity.
